summary: Describes how mail clients and servers using IMAP, POP3 and ACAP can upgrade a plain connection to an encrypted one with TLS. It also defines a PLAIN login method for protocols that lack a simple password command. Later RFCs have updated it.

plainLanguage.summary: Mail programs used to whisper their passwords out loud. This rule lets them first agree to talk through a locked tube, so nobody in the hallway can overhear the secret word.

subtitle: How mail clients upgrade an IMAP, POP3 or ACAP connection to TLS in place, and a PLAIN login for use inside it.

tldr.problem: IMAP, POP3 and ACAP sessions commonly sent passwords and mail in the clear, exposing them to eavesdropping and connection hijacking.
tldr.mechanism: Each protocol gets a command to start a TLS negotiation on the existing connection (STARTTLS for IMAP and ACAP, STLS for POP3), plus rules for cipher suites, server identity checks and refusing clear-text logins until encryption is active. The RFC also defines the PLAIN SASL mechanism.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers can add TLS without a second port, and sites keep their existing password databases. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4616, RFC 7817 and RFC 8314.

today: RFC 2595 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4616, RFC 7817 and RFC 8314, so read those updates alongside it.

sections.title: Why Add TLS to Mail Protocols
sections.content:
The TLS protocol (formerly known as SSL) protects an application protocol from tampering and eavesdropping. The RFC argues that IMAP, POP and ACAP need it because of common connection eavesdropping and hijacking attacks. SASL authentication mechanisms can offer some of this protection, but TLS is complementary to simple authentication-only SASL mechanisms and to deployed clear-text password login commands.

Many sites have a large investment in authentication infrastructure, such as a database holding a one-way function of each user's password. A privacy layer that is not tied to user authentication protects against eavesdropping without forcing a new authentication system or a password change on every user. Because those sites will want simple passwords together with TLS, the RFC also defines the PLAIN SASL mechanism for protocols such as ACAP and SMTP that lack a simple password command.
sections.plainLanguage: Passwords sent as plain text are like shouting your secret across a crowded room. TLS is a way to whisper it instead, without changing the secret itself.

sections.title: Baseline Security Requirements
sections.content:
These rules apply to every implementation of the STARTTLS extension for the three protocols.

  • Cipher suite: implementing TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA is REQUIRED so that any two compliant implementations can be configured to interoperate. All other cipher suites are OPTIONAL.
  • Privacy mode: clients and servers SHOULD have a mode that refuses authentication unless encryption is active by the time of authentication, and ends the connection if encryption is later turned off. Servers SHOULD also keep a backwards-compatible mode that needs only the base protocol's own authentication.
  • Clear-text passwords: implementations MUST be configurable to refuse every clear-text login command or mechanism unless an encryption layer of adequate strength is active.
  • Policy check: both sides MUST check the outcome of STARTTLS and the TLS negotiation. Ignoring this step completely invalidates using TLS for security. What counts as acceptable is a local decision.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must know at least one common lock so any two mail programs can lock the tube together. And a program should refuse to say the password until the lock is really on.

sections.title: Checking the Server's Identity
sections.content:
During the TLS negotiation the client MUST compare the server hostname it used to open the connection with the identity in the server's certificate, to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. It MUST NOT use a hostname obtained from an insecure remote source such as an insecure DNS lookup, and CNAME canonicalization is not done.

Matching is case-insensitive. If a subjectAltName extension of type dNSName is present, it SHOULD be used as the source of the server's identity. A wildcard MAY be the left-most name component, so a certificate name starting with an asterisk then .example.com matches a.example.com and foo.example.com but not example.com. If the certificate holds several names, a match with any one is acceptable.

If the match fails, the client SHOULD either ask the user for explicit confirmation, or end the connection and indicate that the server's identity is suspect.
sections.plainLanguage: Before telling a secret, check that the person you reached is really who you called, not someone wearing a mask.

sections.title: The STARTTLS Commands
sections.content:
Each protocol advertises support as a capability and adds one command that begins a TLS negotiation on the connection already open.

  • IMAP: STARTTLS is listed in the response to CAPABILITY. The command is valid only in the non-authenticated state. The negotiation begins right after the CRLF of the tagged OK, and the client MUST NOT send more commands until the negotiation is complete.
  • POP3: the command is STLS, advertised by the capability name STLS. The POP3 extension mechanism MUST also be implemented. It is permitted only in AUTHORIZATION state, and a -ERR may result if a security layer is already active.
  • ACAP: STARTTLS is listed as a capability in the greeting. After TLS is established the server MUST send a new untagged ACAP greeting.

In all three, the client MUST discard cached information about server capabilities once TLS starts, because a man-in-the-middle could have altered the list beforehand. For IMAP and POP3 the client SHOULD ask again with CAPABILITY or CAPA. The server MAY advertise different capabilities afterwards. The SASL EXTERNAL mechanism MAY be used to authenticate with TLS client credentials, but servers need not support it.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail program says "let's switch to the locked tube", the server agrees, and then both forget what they heard before the switch and ask again.

sections.title: LOGINDISABLED and the PLAIN Mechanism
sections.content:
IMAP's base specification (RFC 2060) requires the LOGIN command, which sends a clear-text password. A server MAY advertise the LOGINDISABLED capability and then answer any LOGIN with a tagged NO. A server that implements STARTTLS MUST support LOGINDISABLED on unencrypted connections, and a compliant client MUST NOT issue LOGIN when it is present. It only helps against passive attacks, since a man-in-the-middle can remove the capability.

The PLAIN SASL mechanism is a single client message: the authorization identity, a NUL character, the authentication identity, a NUL character and the clear-text password. The authorization identity may be empty if it is the same as the authentication identity. It MUST NOT be advertised or used unless a strong encryption layer such as TLS is active, or backwards compatibility dictates otherwise. Text must be UTF-8, and servers MUST accept up to 255 octets for each of the three fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Some servers hide the plain password door until the tube is locked. PLAIN is just "here is my name and my password" and is only safe once the lock is on.

sections.title: Why Not Separate Ports
sections.content:
Separate imaps and pop3s ports were registered for SSL, and the RFC discourages their use in favour of STARTTLS or STLS. It lists several problems with a separate port for a secure variant of a protocol.

  • It leads to a separate URL scheme that intrudes into the user interface.
  • It implies a "secure" or "not secure" model that can mislead. The secure port may use a weak cipher suite, and the normal port might be protected by a SASL mechanism with a security layer. Firewall administrators may be misled into permitting the secure port and blocking the standard one.
  • It pushes clients to implement only two policies, use SSL or do not, when "use TLS when available" is simple with STARTTLS.
  • Port numbers are a limited resource, and doubling their consumption sets a poor precedent.
sections.plainLanguage: Building a second front door just for secure visitors confuses everyone. It is simpler to have one door and a button that locks the hallway.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TLS protects data only while it crosses the network. Messages remain available to server administrators, so TLS is no substitute for end-to-end message security such as MIME security multiparts.

A man-in-the-middle can remove STARTTLS from the capability list or fake a failure response, and can force a down-negotiation to the weakest mechanism or cipher suite available. Clients SHOULD warn the user when session privacy is not active, or be configurable to refuse to proceed without acceptable security, and implementations SHOULD be configurable to refuse weak mechanisms or cipher suites. Everything before the TLS handshake is in the clear, which is why clients MUST discard capabilities cached before it. Clients are encouraged to show clearly when the active encryption is known to be vulnerable, such as keys with 56 bits of entropy or less.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky listener can pretend the locked tube does not exist. So the mail program must notice, warn you, and refuse to talk unless the lock is really there.
